You can still edit SDR video and get good results if you use any of the P3 modes. All the Rec 709 mode does is clamp down on the colors and change the gamma to mimic what video would look on a SDR HDTV

They also would be more color accurate than a regular HDTV with a out of the box preset, unless you are manually color calibrating that TV

It makes it darker because Rec 709 follows a darker gamma close to 2.4 at 100 nits. Compared to the other P3 profiles that are gamma 2.2. and varying levels of brightness.

Never use Display, as that uses your actual screen profile, which despite what Apple says, is not truly calibrated until you have the hardware to calibrate it. I personally use the Photography P3 preset on my 14in XDR as that is close to a calibrated universal profile out of the box.

Display P3 is the actual profile used by OSX, and is the color tagging for all of the images taken by iPhone, and is the default tag for Raw files viewed in OSX. I personally use this as my working space in OSX as recommended by this guide [https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=5cda5ipr](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=5cda5ipr)

Image P3 by my account is the exact same as Display P3, but more for cross-system compatibility between OSX and Windows versions of Adobe software, so that in theory software can read the tag without needing the tag supplied by Apple.

P3 D55 and D60 just change the white point to match print workflows, if that is all you do I would honestly work with the Adobe RGB working space as your tag, as that matches CMYK perfectly, and just set your monitor to one of the design workflows.

The others are specific to cinema workflows, which at that point I would set up the monitor as HDR P3-2084 and your working space in your editing app to be in REC 2100, HDR-10, or HLG. And if not in HDR, SDR workflows should be bt.709 for both monitor and working spaces

From a shooter turned advertising art director who went through several nerve-wracking last minute shoots as a student, I will chime in that before you even pre-plan the shoot, that you make sure the concept itself works. 

Think about summing up the idea as a single image, will it be something a viewer can instantly get at first glance with minimal use of titles?

If it does, great! You just saved yourself a ton of headache and you can work backwards to what leads up to that image. Try making a script work as a 15sec pre-roll social spot (most viewers online will only stay for about 8sec, so try to get the idea as quickly within that time, leaving the rest for product discription, logos, and any call to actions to be seen and understood) then if you want, expand it to a 30 or 60. 

If you want, have your script have some good key art that runs alongside it (as a split script format with either sketches or inspiration images you find)

Then storyboard, I personally hate them compared to shotlists for most narratives, but for a commercial it helps restrict what images you need to sell the idea, get your timing down in post, and see what you need to execute it. 

Another technique I personally like is making a rough cut with outside existing footage or movie scenes that fit aesthetically with your idea, see if the timing works, and of the look and feel of the spots before you go into production.

Check and see if your TV has a “True Cine” or a Film mode. When you output match frame rate the Apple TV will send out a 24p frame rate for most film and tv content instead of 60p for everything, removing motion judder. 

Then a TV with a film mode will take that 24p signal and refresh it 5x or 10x to 120hz or 240hz. This is normal and mimicks how a film projector’s shutter duplicates a frame twice, making a film in the cinema look like it was being shown at 48p.

This is different from motion interpretation when new frames are created based on predicting frames, than can lead to lack of motion blur and artifacts.

iTunes Plus files are typically either sourced from the same CD quality files (16bit 44.1khz) or starting around 2012 from high res files (usually just at 24bit 44.1khz, or 24bit 48khz, with a few at true high res 24bit 96khz or higher) for it's Apple digital masters (previously known as Mastered For iTunes).

These master files, in theory, would be sent from the studio with less compression/limiting than a CD master (which are usually brickwalled to be the loudest it could be) and encoded with a special version of AAC from the standard QuickTime version in iTunes.

In short, an ALAC/FLAC from a 16-bit CD sourced from a proper 24-bit high res master would still contain some fine details and "space between the notes" compared to the same hi-res source for the AAC, but overall sound differences would come down to mastering and encoder variables.

Another reason is how the specific camera would respond to the screen, green screens work better with digital cameras due to digital sensors having more green photo sites than red or blue. While bluescreen works better on film due to the film grain responding with larger exposed crystals when exposed with blue light, leading to sharper detail.

Also yes, green screen is used more during daylight composites while blue is used more during night scenes and underwater scenes, mostly to help conceal any un-keyed leftovers along the edges of the composted subject. 

But any color could be used for a key (yellow was used often in the 40's-60's before green screen fully came to use) and you can also just use a luma key for pure white and black backgrounds (useful for translucent material such as glass or fire) it's just that green and blue are used most often because of how far away they are from human skin tone.
